quote: and it kept access to the variables around it even after the code that made them had finished
problem: The paragraph puts closures and object-to-object inheritance into 'the first version, internally called Mocha'. Neither was in it. Wirfs-Brock & Eich, 'JavaScript: The First 20 Years' (HOPL IV, 2020), says: 'In JavaScript 1.0/1.1 function declarations may occur only at the top level of a script and may not contain nested function declarations' (§3.1). Function expressions were also put off (§2.2), so closures were impossible. Nested functions and function expressions arrived with SpiderMonkey in JavaScript 1.2 (Netscape 4, 1997; §5, Fig 10). The paper also says 'JavaScript 1.0 has no concept of object inheritance' (§3.3). The prototype property came in JavaScript 1.1 (Netscape 3, August 1996). Eich had planned Self-style delegation but 'lacked sufficient time to expose that mechanism in the Mocha prototype' (§2.2). Only first-class functions were there from the start.
fix: "Under the C-like syntax sat Scheme's ideas, some of them finished only in the next two releases: a function was a value that could be stored and passed around like a number, and, once functions could nest (1997), it kept access to the variables around it even after the code that made them had finished (a _closure_). Objects inherited straight from other objects (from 1996), an idea taken from David Ungar and Randall Smith's language _Self_." Source: Wirfs-Brock & Eich, HOPL IV, doi 10.1145/3386327, §2.2, §3.1, §3.3, §5 (https://www.cs.tufts.edu/~nr/cs257/archive/brendan-eich/js-hopl.pdf).
reason: Checked the HOPL IV text. JS 1.0/1.1 allowed function declarations only at top level, with no nested functions or function expressions (Fig 3 lists both as absent from 1.0). Eich added them in the 1996-97 rewrite that became SpiderMonkey, JS 1.2 in Netscape 4. 'JavaScript 1.0 has no concept of object inheritance'; prototype-based inheritance came with 1.1 (Navigator 3). Eich lacked time to expose the delegation mechanism in Mocha. So closures and inheritance are misplaced in 'the first version'.
judge_fix: Replace the 'Under the C-like syntax...' sentence and the next one with: "Under the C-like syntax sat Scheme's ideas, some of them finished only in the next two releases: a function was a value that could be stored and passed around like a number, and, once functions could nest (1997), it kept access to the variables around it even after the code that made them had finished (a _closure_). Objects inherited straight from other objects (from 1996), an idea taken from David Ungar and Randall Smith's language _Self_." Source: Wirfs-Brock and Eich, HOPL IV (2020), section 2.2, section 3 (Fig 3), and the JS 1.2 feature list.

quote: What he got in his first week was a different brief: Marc Andreessen and Bill Joy
problem: This credits Andreessen and Joy with asking for 'the dynamic, interpreted, untyped flexibility of Scheme underneath'. They asked for a 'little language' to go alongside Java. It had to 'look like Java', be object-based without classes, and be easy enough for anyone writing HTML. HOPL §2.2: 'Other than looking like Java, Brendan Eich was free to select most language design details.' The Scheme-style functions and Self-style prototypes were Eich's own choice (Eich, 'Popularity', 2008: 'the diktat ... was that the language must look like Java'). 'In his first week' is also unsupported: Eich 'spent his first month at Netscape officially working in the server group' (HOPL §2.2, note 10).
fix: "What he got instead was a different brief: Marc Andreessen and Bill Joy (Sun co-founder, brought into the Netscape-Sun partnership) wanted a small companion to Java that looked like Java, so that it seemed familiar to working programmers. What went underneath was left to him, and he chose the dynamic, untyped flexibility of Scheme." Source: HOPL IV §2.1–2.2.
reason: HOPL 2.1-2.2: senior managers (Andreessen, Joy) wanted a 'little language' to complement Java that must 'look like Java' and be easy for HTML authors. 'Other than looking like Java, Brendan Eich was free to select most language design details.' Scheme-style functions and Self-style prototypes were his choice. 'First week' is unsupported, and footnote 10 says he spent his first month officially in the server group.
judge_fix: "What he got instead was a different brief: Marc Andreessen and Bill Joy (Sun co-founder, brought into the Netscape-Sun partnership) wanted a small companion to Java: a language that looked like Java, so that it seemed familiar to working programmers, and was easy enough for anyone writing HTML. What went underneath was left to Eich, and he chose the dynamic, interpreted flexibility of Scheme. He had ten days to produce a prototype." This also removes 'untyped' (see 23). Source: HOPL IV 2.1-2.2.

quote: In December 1995 Netscape announced a partnership with Sun Microsystems and renamed it again
problem: The partnership did not begin in December. On 23 May 1995, at Sun's public announcement of Java, Netscape announced it would license Java (HOPL §2.1), and p1 already has Bill Joy in the Netscape-Sun partnership that spring. What happened on 4 December 1995 was a joint Netscape-Sun press release announcing the language as JavaScript (HOPL §3, Appendix F). A careful reader sees p1 and p3 contradict each other.
fix: "On 4 December 1995 Netscape and Sun announced it jointly under a new name, *JavaScript*, the Java name licensed from Sun." Source: HOPL IV §2.1, §3.
reason: HOPL: on 23 May 1995 Netscape announced it would license Java, and p1 already places Joy in the Netscape-Sun partnership that spring. The 4 December 1995 event was the joint Netscape/Sun press release announcing JavaScript. p1 and p3 contradict each other as written.
judge_fix: "In December 1995 Netscape and Sun, by then partners over Java, announced the language jointly and renamed it again, to *JavaScript*." Rest of the paragraph unchanged. Source: HOPL IV 2.1, timeline (23 May, 4 Dec).

quote: JavaScript was originally interpreted a statement at a time by Netscape's engine
problem: Mocha never ran source statement by statement. 'The parser emitted bytecoded instructions rather than a parse tree. The bytecode interpreter was simple and slow' (HOPL §2.2). Bytecode was in fact a requirement of Netscape's LiveWire server team. 'Statement at a time' gives the reader the wrong mechanism, and it clashes with the bytecode interpreter that Fig 12.5 describes for V8.
fix: "JavaScript was originally compiled to simple bytecode and interpreted, slowly, by Netscape's engine: Eich's Mocha, soon rewritten as the engine still called _SpiderMonkey_ today." Source: HOPL IV §2.2.
reason: HOPL 2.2: 'The parser emitted bytecoded instructions rather than a parse tree. The bytecode interpreter was simple and slow.' Bytecode was a LiveWire requirement. 'A statement at a time' names the wrong mechanism and clashes with the bytecode interpreter in Fig 12.5.
judge_fix: "JavaScript was originally compiled to simple bytecode and interpreted, slowly, by Netscape's engine: Eich's Mocha, soon rewritten as the engine still called _SpiderMonkey_ today." Source: HOPL IV 2.2.

quote: By 2008, when Google released V8 alongside the first Chrome browser, JavaScript engines had become aggressive optimising compilers
problem: This dates the change too early. When Chrome shipped in September 2008, no shipping engine had an optimising compiler. V8 1.0 compiled straight to machine code without optimising, as the next sentence and the Fig 12.5 strip say. V8's first optimising compiler, Crankshaft, was announced on 7 December 2010 (Chromium blog, 'A New Crankshaft for V8'). TraceMonkey first shipped in Firefox 3.5 in June 2009. 2008 is when the move to compilers began, not when it was done.
fix: "In 2008, when Google released *V8* alongside the first Chrome browser, JavaScript engines began turning into compilers. V8 began by compiling everything straight to machine code, and its first optimising compiler (Crankshaft) followed in 2010; today's engines, V8 included, run a tiered pipeline..." Source: Chromium blog, 7 Dec 2010 (repost: https://jmesnil.net/weblog/2010/12/07/chromium-blog-a-new-crankshaft-for-v8/).
reason: V8 1.0 (Sept 2008) compiled straight to machine code with inline caches and had no optimising tier. Crankshaft came in Dec 2010, TraceMonkey in Firefox 3.5 (June 2009; HOPL timeline). 'Aggressive optimising compilers' by 2008 is too early, and the next sentence in the same paragraph contradicts it.
judge_fix: "By 2008, when Google released *V8* alongside the first Chrome browser, JavaScript engines had begun turning into compilers. V8 began by compiling everything straight to machine code and added its first optimising compiler in 2010; today's engines, V8 included, run a tiered pipeline from source code to native machine code: ..." (rest unchanged). Source: Chromium blog, 'A New Crankshaft for V8', 7 Dec 2010.

quote: exported from the browser to the server fourteen years after birth
problem: JavaScript ran on servers from its first release. Netscape Enterprise Server 2.0 shipped in March 1996 with JavaScript 1.0 in its LiveWire server-side scripting, and LiveWire's needs shaped Mocha's bytecode design (HOPL §2.2, §3). Microsoft's IIS also ran JScript in Active Server Pages from 1996 (HOPL §4). Node.js in 2009 was the server JavaScript that took hold, not the first.
fix: "...and carried to the server for good, by Node.js, fourteen years after birth." Source: HOPL IV §3 ('Netscape Enterprise Server 2.0 also shipped in March and incorporated JavaScript 1.0 within its LiveWire server-side scripting component'), §4.
reason: HOPL section 3: Netscape Enterprise Server 2.0 (March 1996) shipped JavaScript 1.0 in LiveWire, and LiveWire shaped Mocha's bytecode (2.2). 'Exported to the server fourteen years after birth' is false as worded. Node 2009 is when it took hold.
judge_fix: "...shipped before specification, and carried to the server in earnest by Node.js fourteen years after birth."

quote: given an unrelated marketing name to ride a competitor's hype
problem: Sun was Netscape's partner, not its competitor. Netscape licensed Java in May 1995, Andreessen's rallying cry was 'Netscape plus Java kills Windows', and the two companies announced JavaScript together on 4 December 1995 (HOPL §2.1, §3). The chapter's own p3 calls it a partnership, so the closing paragraph contradicts it.
fix: "given an unrelated marketing name to ride a partner's hype"
reason: Sun was Netscape's partner (Java licence May 1995, joint announcement Dec 1995), and the chapter's own p3 says partnership and 'Sun's Java publicity'. 'Competitor' is wrong and contradicts p3.
judge_fix: "given an unrelated marketing name to ride a partner's hype"

quote: do not attach this cookie to cross-site POST requests; only to top-level navigations
problem: This is the caption (ch12-security-p7). SameSite=Lax sends the cookie only on top-level navigations that use a safe method such as GET (following a link). A cross-site form POST, which is exactly the attack the figure draws, is also a top-level navigation and gets no Lax cookie. As written, 'only to top-level navigations' suggests Lax would let the figure's auto-submitted POST through.
fix: "`SameSite=Lax` means: attach this cookie to a cross-site request only when it is a top-level navigation that uses GET, such as following a link; never to a cross-site POST." Source: MDN Set-Cookie SameSite (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Set-Cookie#samesitesamesite-value); RFC 6265bis 'Lax' enforcement (safe methods only).
reason: Real. Lax sends the cookie on cross-site requests only for top-level navigations using a safe method (GET), so a top-level cross-site form POST gets none. 'Only to top-level navigations' is loose, though the first clause ('do not attach to cross-site POST') already states the point. Caption of kept-original Fig 12.10, so the owner decides. Same as 39.
judge_fix: "`SameSite=Lax` means: on a cross-site request, attach this cookie only when it is a top-level navigation that uses GET, such as following a link; never on a cross-site POST." Source: MDN Set-Cookie SameSite; RFC 6265bis Lax enforcement.

quote: a niche by 2000, obsolete by 2010, removed from browsers entirely by 2017
problem: Not all browsers had dropped it by 2017. Chrome dropped NPAPI in 2015 and Firefox 52 in March 2017, but Firefox ESR 52 kept it into 2018. Safari dropped all NPAPI plug-ins except Flash only in Safari 12 (September 2018), and Internet Explorer 11 kept running the Java plug-in. Oracle deprecated the plug-in in JDK 9 (2017) and removed it in JDK 11 (2018). The Fig 12.1 strip repeats the claim: 'browsers had dropped the plugin interface they needed by 2017'.
fix: Prose: "a niche by 2000, obsolete by 2010, and cut loose by Java itself in 2018, when Oracle removed the browser plug-in." Strip: "Applets faded, and Java removed its browser plug-in in 2018." Sources: https://www.java.com/en/download/help/jdk9_plugin.html; Oracle JDK 11 'Removed Tools and Components' (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/migrate/removed-tools-and-components.html); Safari 12 NPAPI removal (Wikipedia NPAPI).
reason: 'Removed from browsers entirely by 2017' overclaims. Chrome dropped NPAPI in 2015 and Firefox 52 in March 2017, but Safari kept it until Safari 12 (Sept 2018), Firefox ESR 52 ran to 2018, and Oracle removed the Java browser plug-in in JDK 11 (2018). The Fig 12.1 strip repeats the claim. Same as 22.
judge_fix: Prose: "a niche by 2000, obsolete by 2010, dropped by the major browsers between 2015 and 2018." Strip: "Applets faded, and the major browsers dropped the plugin interface they needed between 2015 and 2018."

quote: microtasks arrived with Promises
problem: The microtask queue entered the HTML/DOM specs for Mutation Observers in about 2011–12. Promises were moved onto it in 2013, 'for pretty much the same reasons as with MutationObserver' (W3C bug 22296; W3C bug 24725 'Use the microtask queue for MutationObserver'). Promises are now the main user of microtasks, but they did not bring them.
fix: "...microtasks arrived in the 2010s, and Promises are their main user."
reason: The microtask queue entered the HTML/DOM specs for MutationObserver (c. 2012); Promises were moved onto it later. Promises are now the main user but did not bring microtasks. A cheap, safe correction. Same as 27.
judge_fix: "The event loop's shape has been the same since 1995; microtasks arrived in the 2010s, and Promises are now their main user."

quote: Within five years Node had become the default backend for Silicon Valley startups
problem: This overclaims. By 2014 Node was popular, but nothing supports calling it 'the default': Rails, Python and Java stacks were at least as common among startups. As it stands it is an unsourced superlative.
fix: "Within five years Node had become a common backend for startups; within ten it had taken a large share of server-side work."
reason: 'The default backend for Silicon Valley startups' is an unsourced superlative. Rails, Python and Java stacks were at least as common in 2014. Same as 32.
judge_fix: "Within five years Node had become a mainstream backend for startups; within ten it had taken a large share of server-side work."

quote: the framework computes the minimum set of DOM mutations and applies them together
problem: No mainstream framework computes the minimum. React's reconciliation is an O(n) heuristic, chosen because a truly minimal tree diff is O(n³) (React docs, 'Reconciliation'). Svelte compiles direct updates and does no diffing at all.
fix: "the framework works out a small set of DOM mutations and applies them together"
reason: React's reconciliation is a linear heuristic by design (a minimal tree diff is O(n^3)), and Svelte does no diffing. 'Computes the minimum set' is wrong for the frameworks named. Same as 33.
judge_fix: "the framework works out only the DOM changes the new data needs and applies them together, so reads rarely land between the writes."

quote: it runs a hundred kilobytes of code on your machine
problem: This understates by about five times. The median page ships 558 KB of JavaScript on mobile and 613 KB on desktop (HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2024, Page Weight), and news sites usually ship more.
fix: "it runs hundreds of kilobytes of code on your machine" Source: https://almanac.httparchive.org/en/2024/page-weight.
reason: Median page JavaScript is several hundred KB (HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2024, about 560-610 KB), so 'a hundred kilobytes' understates by roughly five times. Free fix.
judge_fix: "it runs hundreds of kilobytes of code on your machine"

quote: A typical strict policy
problem: In current usage (web.dev 'Mitigate XSS with a strict CSP'; the CSP Level 3 spec), 'strict' means a policy built on nonces or hashes. An allowlist of hosts like this example is the kind the Google study 'CSP Is Dead, Long Live CSP!' (CCS 2016) found bypassable in most deployments. The chapter's own Fig 12.11 strip says 'A strict policy admits chosen inline scripts by a fresh random nonce', so the two passages use 'strict' for different things.
fix: "A typical allowlist policy: `script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com; style-src 'self'` means..."
reason: The chapter's own Fig 12.11 strip uses 'strict policy' for nonce/hash policies, which is the current meaning (CSP Level 3, web.dev). The p8 example is a host allowlist, the weaker kind. Same word, two meanings within a few lines.
judge_fix: "A typical allowlist policy: `script-src 'self' https://cdn.example.com; style-src 'self'` means: ..." (rest unchanged).

quote: If an attacker injects a `<script src="evil.com/x.js">`
problem: In HTML, src="evil.com/x.js" is a relative path. It resolves to /evil.com/x.js on the page's own origin, which 'self' would allow, so the worked example does not show what the sentence claims. In a section that teaches origins, a programmer reading closely will catch this.
fix: "If an attacker injects a `<script src="https://evil.com/x.js">`, the browser sees that `evil.com` is not in the policy..."
reason: In an HTML attribute, src="evil.com/x.js" is a relative path that resolves to the page's own origin, which 'self' allows. In the section that teaches origins this is a real slip, and the repair is two words.
judge_fix: "If an attacker injects a `<script src="https://evil.com/x.js">`, the browser sees that `evil.com` is not in the policy and refuses to load the script."

quote: were retrofitted over thirty years in response to attacks that worked
problem: The same-origin policy appears in this list of retrofits, but p2 says it was 'introduced in Netscape 2.0, the same release that shipped JavaScript itself'. It was there from day one, not retrofitted after attacks.
fix: "The security mechanisms that surround it (the same-origin policy from the first release, then CSRF tokens, Content Security Policy and more) were added over thirty years, most of them in response to attacks that worked."
reason: p2 and the Fig 12.8 strip say the same-origin policy arrived with JavaScript, so listing it among mechanisms 'retrofitted ... in response to attacks that worked' contradicts them. (Wikipedia dates it to Navigator 2.02 in 1996, shortly after 2.0; 'almost from the start' avoids the exact release.) Same as 34.
judge_fix: "The security mechanisms that surround it (the same-origin policy almost from the start, then CSRF tokens, Content Security Policy and more) were added over thirty years, mostly in response to attacks that worked."

quote: whose browser had become the market-share leader through 1994 and 1995
problem: Netscape was not the leader through 1994. Navigator was first widely distributed in October 1994, and 'by early 1995 Netscape Navigator had achieved its initial goal and was rapidly displacing Mosaic' (HOPL §2).
fix: "Netscape, whose browser had overtaken Mosaic as the market leader by early 1995, wanted something different."
reason: Navigator first shipped in October 1994, and HOPL says that by early 1995 it was displacing Mosaic. 'Leader through 1994 and 1995' is a slight overstatement. Cheap fix.
judge_fix: "Netscape, whose browser had overtaken Mosaic as the market leader by early 1995, wanted something different."

quote: XSS still appears every year on the OWASP Top 10
problem: This is the caption (ch12-security-p5). The OWASP Top 10 is not yearly: it is revised every three to four years (2003, 2004, 2007, 2010, 2013, 2017, 2021, 2025). Since 2021 XSS has had no entry of its own; it sits inside Injection (A03:2021, A05:2025).
fix: "Even so, XSS is still on the OWASP Top 10, inside its Injection category." Source: https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A05_2025-Injection/.
reason: Real. The OWASP Top 10 is revised every few years (2017, 2021, 2025), not yearly, and since 2021 XSS sits inside Injection. This is the caption of kept-original Fig 12.9, so the owner decides. Same as 35.
judge_fix: "Even so, XSS is still on the OWASP Top 10, inside its Injection category." Source: owasp.org/Top10 (A03:2021 Injection).

quote: browser executes the injected script as same-origin with example.com
problem: The attacked URL in the same panel is search.example.com. By the rule Fig 12.8 has just taught (shop.example.com is not www.example.com), that is a different origin from example.com, so the label contradicts the lesson before it.
fix: "③ browser executes the injected script as same-origin with search.example.com"
reason: Real. The panel's URL is search.example.com, which by Fig 12.8's own rule is not example.com. Kept-original figure label. Same as 36.
judge_fix: "③ browser executes the injected script as same-origin with search.example.com"

problem: ch12-browser-p2 'removed from browsers entirely by 2017', and the fig-12-1 How it works strip 'browsers had dropped the plugin interface they needed by 2017': this is not accurate. Chrome 45 dropped NPAPI in September 2015 and Firefox 52 in March 2017, but Firefox 52 ESR ran the Java plugin until 2018, Safari dropped NPAPI only in Safari 12 (September 2018), and Internet Explorer 11 ran applets through the ActiveX Java plugin until IE was retired in June 2022. Oracle deprecated the Applet API in JDK 9 (2017) and removed the browser plugin in JDK 11 (2018). A wording that holds: 'dropped by the major browsers between 2015 and 2018' or 'deprecated by Oracle in 2017'.
reason: Same as 10: the 2017 claim is too early for Safari (2018), Firefox ESR 52 and Oracle's JDK 11 removal (2018).
judge_fix: Prose: "dropped by the major browsers between 2015 and 2018." Strip: "...the major browsers dropped the plugin interface they needed between 2015 and 2018."

problem: ch12-browser-p3 'small, untyped snippets', read against p2 'a real language that checked its types': this contradicts what the book taught earlier. ch7-types-p2 classes JavaScript as dynamically typed: it does check types, at runtime, and dies with a TypeError. The word that sits closest to 'untyped' is ch5-portability-p7's 'typeless', which means BCPL and B, where every value is a bare machine word. A careful reader may take JavaScript to be typeless like BCPL. What it actually lacked was declared types and a compile-time check. A wording that holds: 'small snippets with no type declarations', or 'dynamically typed snippets'.
reason: ch7-types-p2 teaches that JavaScript is dynamically typed (it checks types at run time), and 'untyped' reads as typeless, as in BCPL. p2's contrast ('a real language that checked its types') overstates it. Two places: browser-p3 and eich-p1. The eich-p1 fix in 2 already drops the word.
judge_fix: browser-p3: "small snippets with no type declarations that any HTML author could add without compilers...". eich-p1: "the dynamic, interpreted flexibility of Scheme". Optionally browser-p2: "a real language that checked its types before running".

problem: ch12-eich-p3: 'In December 1995 Netscape announced a partnership with Sun Microsystems'. Netscape had agreed to license Java from Sun in May 1995 (announced at SunWorld on 23 May 1995). The event of 4 December 1995 was the joint Netscape and Sun announcement of JavaScript, made under a trademark licence from Sun. It was not a new partnership, and p1 already treats the partnership as existing in spring 1995.
reason: Duplicate of 3. The partnership dates from May 1995; December 1995 was the joint announcement.
judge_fix: As in 3: "In December 1995 Netscape and Sun, by then partners over Java, announced the language jointly and renamed it again, to *JavaScript*."

problem: ch12-eich-p1: 'What he got in his first week was a different brief'. The timing is not verified. Eich's own accounts give the 'must look like Java' order from management in spring 1995 without naming a week. The HOPL history (Wirfs-Brock and Eich, 2020) may say he was first put on server work. Check it against the source.
reason: Duplicate of 2. HOPL note 10 says his first month was officially in the server group, and the 'little language' brief came from senior managers during spring 1995, not a stated 'first week'.
judge_fix: As in 2: drop 'in his first week' and use 'What he got instead was a different brief'.

problem: ch12-loop-p4 'microtasks arrived with Promises': in browsers the microtask queue came first with MutationObserver (shipped in 2012). Native Promises followed (2014, standardised in ES2015) and used the queue that already existed. 'Promises made microtasks central' would be safer.
reason: Duplicate of 12. MutationObserver (c. 2012) used the microtask queue before Promises moved onto it.
judge_fix: As in 12: "microtasks arrived in the 2010s, and Promises are now their main user."

problem: ch12-node-p1: 'interpreted a statement at a time' may be wrong. Mocha (and SpiderMonkey after it) compiled each script to bytecode and interpreted the bytecode. It did not interpret statement by statement.
reason: Duplicate of 4. Mocha compiled to bytecode (HOPL 2.2).
judge_fix: As in 4: "originally compiled to simple bytecode and interpreted, slowly, by Netscape's engine".

problem: ch12-node-p1: 'By 2008 ... JavaScript engines had become aggressive optimising compilers' looks too early. V8 in 2008 had only a fast non-optimising compiler (full-codegen, with inline caches). Its first optimising compiler, Crankshaft, shipped in December 2010, and TraceMonkey arrived in 2008-09.
reason: Duplicate of 5. V8 1.0 had no optimising compiler (Crankshaft, Dec 2010).
judge_fix: As in 5: "JavaScript engines had begun turning into compilers", then V8's optimising compiler arrived in 2010.

problem: Fig 12.6 How it works: 'libuv asks the OS which ones are ready (epoll ..., kqueue ..., IOCP on Windows)'. That describes epoll and kqueue, but IOCP is completion-based: it reports finished operations, not ready sockets.
reason: Accurate: epoll and kqueue report readiness, while IOCP reports completed operations. libuv emulates readiness on Windows. The strip lumps them under 'which ones are ready'. Low severity, but the repair is a few words.
judge_fix: "...libuv asks the OS to say when they are ready or done (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS and BSD, IOCP on Windows)."

problem: ch12-node-p4: 'Within five years Node had become the default backend for Silicon Valley startups' is probably an overstatement for 2014, when Rails, Python and Java were still at least as common.
reason: Duplicate of 13.
judge_fix: As in 13: "Within five years Node had become a mainstream backend for startups; within ten it had taken a large share of server-side work."

problem: ch12-dom-p3: 'the framework computes the minimum set of DOM mutations' overstates. React's reconciliation is a heuristic diff (linear, keyed) and makes no promise of a minimum. Svelte does not diff at all: it compiles direct, targeted updates. 'a small set' or 'only the changes needed' would be safe.
reason: Duplicate of 14.
judge_fix: As in 14: "the framework works out only the DOM changes the new data needs and applies them together".

problem: p10 says the same-origin policy was 'retrofitted over thirty years in response to attacks that worked', but p2 and the Fig 12.8 strip say it shipped in Netscape 2.0 together with JavaScript. A reader notices the contradiction (p1's 'invented over thirty years' is fine).
reason: Duplicate of 18. p10 lists the same-origin policy as retrofitted while p2 and the Fig 12.8 strip say it shipped with JavaScript.
judge_fix: As in 18: "(the same-origin policy almost from the start, then CSRF tokens, Content Security Policy and more) were added over thirty years, mostly in response to attacks that worked."

problem: p5 caption: 'XSS still appears every year on the OWASP Top 10'. The list comes out every few years (2017, 2021, 2025), not yearly, and since 2021 XSS has been folded into the Injection category instead of standing on its own.
reason: Duplicate of 20, a real error in the caption of kept-original Fig 12.9.
judge_fix: As in 20: "Even so, XSS is still on the OWASP Top 10, inside its Injection category."

problem: kept-original (Fig 12.9), low severity: step 3 of the reflected row says 'same-origin with example.com', but the URL is search.example.com. Fig 12.8 has just taught that a different subdomain is a different origin. The prose can avoid echoing the slip.
reason: Duplicate of 21, a real label slip in kept-original Fig 12.9. The prose does not echo it.
judge_fix: As in 21: "same-origin with search.example.com".

problem: kept-original (Fig 12.10), pedantic: the form action "bank.com/transfer" has no scheme, so it is a relative URL and would resolve under evil.com. A real attack needs https://bank.com/transfer.
reason: Real, and the same slip as 17: an HTML action="bank.com/transfer" is a relative URL. It sits in a kept-original figure label, so the owner decides. The prose use in p6 is host shorthand and is fine.
judge_fix: In Fig 12.10 step 3: <form action="https://bank.com/transfer" method="POST">

problem: p7: SameSite=Lax also withholds the cookie on cross-site image, frame and fetch requests, not only on POSTs, and it attaches the cookie only on top-level GET navigations. 'Only to top-level navigations' can be read as including a top-level cross-site POST form submission, which Lax blocks.
reason: Duplicate of 9. Lax omits the cookie on cross-site images, frames, fetch and POST, and sends it only on top-level GET navigations. The caption wording is loose but not wrong. Kept-original caption.
judge_fix: As in 9: "on a cross-site request, attach this cookie only when it is a top-level navigation that uses GET, such as following a link; never on a cross-site POST."

problem: p10, low severity: 'exported from the browser to the server fourteen years after birth'. Netscape's LiveWire already ran server-side JavaScript in 1996. Node.js (2009) is when it went mainstream, so 'went mainstream on the server' would be safer.
reason: Duplicate of 6. LiveWire ran server-side JavaScript in 1996.
judge_fix: As in 6: "...and carried to the server in earnest by Node.js fourteen years after birth."

quote: with .then() and .catch() chained horizontally
problem: Wrong word. In Fig 12.4 the promise chain runs down the page, one `.then` per line. The thing that marches sideways is the callback pyramid this sentence is contrasting with. "Horizontally" says the opposite of the picture.
fix: "...with `.then()` and `.catch()` chained one after another in a flat list instead of nested."
reason: Fig 12.4 shows the promise chain as a flat vertical list. The thing that marches sideways is the callback pyramid just described. 'Horizontally' points the wrong way.
judge_fix: with `.then()` and `.catch()` chained one after another in a flat list instead of nested.

quote: In December 1995 Netscape announced a partnership with Sun Microsystems and renamed it again
problem: p1 already has Bill Joy "brought into the Netscape-Sun partnership" in April–May 1995, so the partnership exists before p3 announces it in December. The reader cannot tell whether there were two deals.
fix: "In December 1995, in a joint announcement with Sun Microsystems, Netscape renamed it again, to *JavaScript*."
reason: p1 puts Bill Joy inside a 'Netscape-Sun partnership' in April 1995. p3 then 'announced a partnership' in December, which reads like a second deal. The December event was the joint JavaScript announcement. Minor, but cheap to fix.
judge_fix: In December 1995, in a joint announcement with Sun Microsystems, Netscape renamed it again, to *JavaScript*.

quote: given an unrelated marketing name to ride a competitor's hype
problem: §02 presents Sun as Netscape's partner: a joint deal, and Sun held the Java trademark that Netscape licensed. The closing paragraph now calls Sun a competitor.
fix: "given an unrelated marketing name to ride a partner's hype" (or "to ride Java's hype").
reason: §02 treats Sun as Netscape's partner and Java's owner. 'A competitor's hype' contradicts that, and p3 itself says 'Sun's Java publicity'.
judge_fix: given an unrelated marketing name to ride Java's hype

quote: It should run instantly, fail loudly without crashing the browser
problem: §02 and the insight strip make JavaScript's defining quirk implicit coercion, "silently turning one type into another". The language was built to forgive, not to fail loudly. A careful reader sees the contradiction two sections later.
fix: "It should run instantly, fail without taking the browser down with it, and be easy enough..."
reason: JavaScript's defining trait in this chapter is silent coercion and forgiving behaviour. 'Fail loudly' contradicts that two sections later and has no historical backing.
judge_fix: It should run instantly, fail without taking the browser down with it, and be easy enough for a designer who had learned HTML over a weekend to pick up.

quote: meant JavaScript could never expose the difference
problem: "The difference" has no referent: between what and what? The sentence has to be read twice and still does not land. It also repeats p2's "no integers (only floating-point numbers...)", so the no-integer point is made twice.
fix: "`0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3` is just IEEE 754 (Chapter 2's floating-point section), but because every number is a 64-bit float, JavaScript has no exact integer type to fall back on."
reason: 'The difference' has no referent. BigInt (ES2020) also makes 'could never expose' false today. The no-integer point is already in p2, so the sentence should only say what the missing integer type meant for 0.1 + 0.2.
judge_fix: `0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3` is just IEEE 754 (Chapter 2, Section 06), but because every number was a 64-bit float, early JavaScript had no exact integer type to fall back on.

quote: It was genuine elegance underneath surprising syntactic awkwardness
problem: This is an aphorism closer ("the shape of any language born in ten days under the wrong brief"), and "syntactic" is the wrong word. None of the listed flaws is syntax: missing classes, no integers and implicit coercion are semantics. The C-like syntax is presented as the familiar part.
fix: Cut the sentence. The paragraph ends on the coercion clause, and the insight strip (p6) already draws the ten-day lesson.
reason: The sentence is an aphorism closer that restates what the paragraph and the p6 strip already say. 'Syntactic' is also the wrong word: the listed flaws (no classes, no integers, coercion) are semantic, and the C-like syntax is the familiar part.
judge_fix: Cut the sentence 'It was genuine elegance underneath surprising syntactic awkwardness: the shape of any language born in ten days under the wrong brief.' The paragraph ends on '...cursed.' Also cut 'He delivered.' only if desired (finding 45 is rejected as voice).

quote: None of this was inevitable. All of it became, by accumulation, the shape of the modern web.
problem: The paragraph closes on a two-fragment aphorism. It also reuses p1's phrase "over thirty years in response to attacks that worked" almost word for word, summarising what was just said.
fix: End the paragraph at "...in response to attacks that worked." and drop the two closing sentences. Or vary the p1 echo: "were added one attack at a time."
reason: The final two fragments are a stamped aphorism. 'Retrofitted over thirty years in response to attacks that worked' also repeats p1's wording almost exactly, so the chapter ends on a restatement.
judge_fix: Replace the last two sentences with a change to the previous one: '...were retrofitted, one attack at a time, over thirty years.' End the paragraph there.

quote: An origin is a scheme, a host and a port, and two URLs share one only if all three match
problem: The definition and the three one-change examples appear three times: p2 (a./b.example.com, http/https, :80/:8080), the picture, and the caption ("http for https, shop for www, 8443 for 443"). Per the brief, the prose keeps it and the caption names the picture.
fix: Caption: "One origin split into its three parts, and three URLs that each change one of them; the path never counts, so only the first is the same origin."
reason: The caption restates p2's definition and its three one-change examples, and the picture shows them again. Law 3 wants a caption that names the picture. The finding's suggested caption says 'each change one part', which is wrong because the http URL differs in two places.
judge_fix: The origin https://www.example.com split into scheme, host and port, and three other URLs each compared with it: the path never counts, so only the first is the same origin.

quote: The CSS is parsed into another tree (the CSSOM).
problem: CSS is never explained anywhere before this point. Ch11 only mentions "stylesheets" once, in passing. The style and layout stages, and the caption's width and colour changes, all lean on it.
fix: "The CSS (the style rules that set each element's size, colour and position) is parsed into another tree (the CSSOM)."
reason: This is the first use of CSS anywhere in the book (the only earlier 'stylesheet' hits are <link> tags). The style stage, the CSSOM and the caption's width and colour changes all depend on it. A short gloss fixes it.
judge_fix: The CSS (the style rules that set each element's size, colour and position) is parsed into another tree (the CSSOM).

quote: watched the progress bar on a file upload in a browser and realised
problem: The story image is never cashed out. Nothing says why a progress bar would show that thread-per-connection servers are the wrong shape: the browser had to keep asking a busy server how much had arrived. The reader stops at the leap.
fix: Cash it out with one clause: "watched a browser's upload progress bar, which could only learn how far the upload had got by asking the server again and again, and realised...". Or cut the image: "In 2009 a developer named Ryan Dahl realised..."
reason: The progress-bar image is never cashed out. Dahl's own account (SiliconANGLE 2013, https://siliconangle.com/blog/2013/04/01/the-birth-of-node-where-did-it-come-from-creator-ryan-dahl-shares-the-history/) says a progress bar works by the browser repeatedly asking the server how much has arrived, and the server has to answer while a long upload is still running. Frameworks of the time assumed each request returned instantly.
judge_fix: In 2009 a developer named *Ryan Dahl* watched a browser's file-upload progress bar, which works by asking the server again and again how much has arrived, and realised that the standard server-side approaches (...) were exactly the wrong shape for systems with many slow connections.

quote: ③ browser executes the injected script as same-origin with example.com
problem: The reflected example's URL is https://search.example.com. Its origin is search.example.com, not example.com. p2 has just taught that a.example.com and b.example.com are different origins, so the figure contradicts the section.
fix: Owner call (kept original): "③ browser executes the injected script as same-origin with search.example.com".
reason: Real factual slip in a kept-original figure. The reflected example's URL is https://search.example.com/..., so the injected script runs as same-origin with search.example.com, not example.com. p2 has just taught that subdomains are different origins.
judge_fix: Owner call (kept original, Fig 12.9, reflected step 3): '③ browser executes the injected script as same-origin with search.example.com'.

quote: Take one task, run it to the end, run every microtask, render if a frame is due
problem: The strip's first bullet repeats the last sentence of p2 ("pull one task off the macrotask queue, run it to completion, drain the microtask queue completely, optionally render, repeat"). Only the 16 ms figure is new.
fix: Replace the bullet with "*The render step.* The browser renders only when a frame is due, about every 16 ms on a 60 Hz screen."
reason: The strip's first bullet is the last sentence of p2 almost word for word. Only the 16 ms figure is new.
judge_fix: *The render step.* The browser renders only when a frame is due, about every 16 ms on a 60 Hz screen.

quote: Understanding this pipeline is the difference between a page that holds 60 frames per second and a page that stutters.
problem: An aphorism closer. The paragraph also opens with a "Not X. Y." reveal ("Loading a web page does not 'show' the HTML. The browser runs...").
fix: Open: "When a page loads, the browser runs the fetched bytes through a five-stage pipeline...". Close by handing to the figure: "Which stages a change re-runs decides whether the page holds 60 frames per second (Fig 12.7)."
reason: 'Understanding this pipeline is the difference between...' announces importance, which law 2 cuts. Naming the 60 fps stake is fine; it should hand off to the figure instead. The 'does not show the HTML' opener is a taste matter and is left alone.
judge_fix: Replace the last sentence with: Which stages a change re-runs decides whether the page holds 60 frames per second (Fig 12.7).

quote: A typical strict policy
problem: The p8 example (an origin allowlist) is called "strict", while Fig 12.11's strip uses "a strict policy" for the nonce-or-hash kind. One word, two meanings in one section.
fix: "A typical allowlist policy:"
reason: p8 calls an origin allowlist 'strict'. The Fig 12.11 strip uses 'a strict policy' for nonce or hash policies, which is the standard industry meaning. Allowlists are the weaker kind. One word, two meanings in one section.
judge_fix: A typical allowlist policy:

quote: An origin is the triple (scheme, host, port)
problem: "Scheme" in the URL sense is never glossed. The reader last met Scheme as the Lisp dialect in §02, and the URL meaning has to be inferred from the examples.
fix: "An origin is the triple (scheme, host, port), the scheme being the `https` or `http` at the front of the URL, and..."
reason: Ch11 calls this part of a URL the 'protocol', and the only earlier 'Scheme' is the Lisp dialect in §02. The examples and picture make it inferable, but one clause links it to Ch11's word.
judge_fix: An origin is the triple (scheme, host, port), the scheme being the protocol at the front of the URL, `https` or `http`, and two URLs share an origin if and only if all three match exactly.

quote: Change any one, `http` for `https`, `shop` for `www`, 8443 for 443
problem: The caption gives http-for-https as a change to one part. The picture and the strip say that URL "differs in two places" (scheme and default port).
fix: Covered by the caption rewrite above. Otherwise: "(`http` for `https` changes the default port too)".
reason: The caption lists http-for-https as a change to one part. The picture and the strip say that URL differs in two (scheme and default port). Real but small, and the same rewrite as finding 11 repairs it.
judge_fix: Covered by the finding 11 caption: 'The origin https://www.example.com split into scheme, host and port, and three other URLs each compared with it: the path never counts, so only the first is the same origin.'

quote: even when an XSS injection has already put it in the page
problem: The key-term highlight (span.key-term) sits on "XSS" in this caption, its fourth appearance. The term is defined in p4, where it carries only <strong> on "cross-site scripting". The new-term styling lands in the wrong place.
fix: Move the key-term span to the first "XSS" in p4 and make the caption's "XSS" plain text.
reason: The glossary has a separate 'xss' entry. The build and book.js anchor the first element whose text normalises to 'xss' in document order. In p4 'XSS' is plain text, so the caption span in p9 gets term-xss, and the glossary link for XSS jumps into the CSP caption instead of the definition.
judge_fix: In ch12-security-p4 write: cross-site scripting (XSS). In ch12-security-p9 make 'XSS' plain text. Rebuild the glossary.
